newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korean lawmaker questioned on loans scandal.
newsitem.headline: S.Korean lawmaker questioned on loans scandal.

text.p: South Korean prosecutors on Friday began questioning a prominent opposition lawmaker at the start of a renewed inquiry into a group of politicians over the Hanbo loans scandal.
Analysts said the probe could lead to a shift in the country's political alignment.

A prosecution official said Kim Yong-hwan, secretary-general of the United Liberal Democrats (ULD), was being investigated to find out if he had accepted money illegally from the founder of the troubled Hanbo Group.
The ULD is one of the two main opposition parties.
Kim is among 33 politicians, including 20 members of parliament, the prosecutors said they would question in the next two weeks in connection with a loans scandal involving Hanbo.
"They include major figures and I am afraid this might touch off a political big bang," said a member of the ruling New Korea Party who asked not to be identified.
"The biggest casualty will be political apathy. If lawmakers are probed one after another, the credibility of political establishments will be seriously damaged," he said.
Hanbo founder Chung Tae-soo and his aides have told prosecutors that they gave money to the 33 as "political funds" but denied bribing them, senior prosecutor Shim Je-ryoon said.
The prosecutors charged that Chung had bribed politicians and bankers to keep loans rolling into Hanbo's steelmaking flagship, which collapsed in January.
They alleged that Chung diverted millions of dollars from the bank loans earmarked for investment and used it to buy influence.

Prosecutors said another opposition member of parliament, Kim Sang-hyun of the National Congress for New Politics, had agreed to report to the prosecution office for questioning on Friday over the scandal.

Among the 20 lawmakers are 13 from the ruling party, including Kim Deog-ryong, a member of President Kim Young-sam's inner circle. He would probably report to the prosecution on Saturday, the prosecutors said.
Both Kim Sang-hyun and Kim Deog-ryong have said they will seek to run in presidential elections in December.
"I suspect there might be a conspiracy against me," Kim Deog-ryong told reporters, denying he took money from Chung.
Shim said his investigation team wanted to question the three senior politicians first as Chung told a parliamentary hearing this week that his aides delivered his money to them.
All three politicians have denied taking money from Chung.
Chung is on trial on bribery and other charges along with nine others, including three close associates of President Kim, in connection with the collapse of Hanbo Steel Co.
The parliamentary hearing, being broadcast live from a jail where Chung and some others are being held, sparked public calls that corrupt links between businessmen and politicians must be revealed.

"A political realignment has been expected after this year's presidential election. The Hanbo scandal and conflicts caused by the probe could speed up a restructuring," said Shin Jung-hyun, political science professor at Seoul's Kyunghee University.
The loans scandal that has rocked the economy and damaged President Kim's credibility threatened to foil his plan to install one of his proteges as his successor, Shin said.
The constitution bars the president from seeking re-election.
The opposition on Friday accused the prosecution of trying to divert public attention away from a probe into allegations that the president's second son accepted kickbacks.
The son, Kim Hyun-chul, is due to appear at the 45-day parliamentary hearing later this month.
